 7 Big Social Security Changes That Will Affect Retirees in 2027
 Josh Koebert 2026년 11월 14일 토 오전 10:00 UTC 0 
Every fall, the Social Security Administration (SSA) grabs headlines with its annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), the percentage bump designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation. But the COLA is just one of several moving parts that reset each January. A handful of other, less-publicized changes can matter just as much, especially for people still working, people nearing full retirement age (FRA, the age at which you qualify for 100% of your benefit), or those earning near the top of the pay scale.
For 2027, the SSA has confirmed a batch of adjustments that go well beyond the headline COLA number. Some of these changes will put more money in your pocket when living on Social Security . Others mean higher taxes or stricter thresholds for people still in the workforce. 
 Here's what's changing, how it compares with 2026, and who it affects.

 1. Social Security COLA increases benefits by 3.6% in 2027
The SSA announced a 3.6% COLA for 2027, which takes effect with January 2027 benefits for nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, who number about 7.3 million, see their increase start with payments on December 31, 2026, according to the SSA. On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by about $75 per month, the agency says.
That's useful context, but it's not the whole story. The COLA adjusts existing benefits; it doesn't change the rules that determine how much new retirees can qualify for, how much high earners pay into the system, or how much working beneficiaries can earn before their checks are temporarily reduced. Those rules are adjusting too, and in some cases, the changes are more consequential than the COLA itself.

 2. Higher Social Security earnings limits let working retirees earn more
If you claim Social Security before reaching your full retirement age and keep working, the SSA applies an earnings test that can temporarily withhold part of your benefit if you earn above a set threshold. For 2027, that threshold is getting more generous.
For people who won't reach full retirement age at any point in 2027, the annual exempt amount rises to $25,560, up from $24,480 in 2026, according to the SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet. Earnings above that limit trigger a withholding of $1 in benefits for every $2 earned over the cap.
For people who reach full retirement age sometime in 2027, a higher, separate limit applies: $67,920, up from $65,160 in 2026. That higher limit only counts earnings in the months before you hit FRA, and the withholding rate is lower: just $1 withheld for every $3 earned above the limit. Once you reach FRA, the earnings test disappears entirely. No limit applies for the rest of that year or afterward, per the SSA.
The practical consequence: working beneficiaries under FRA can earn more in 2027 before any benefits get withheld. It's also worth noting that money withheld under the earnings test isn't gone for good. The SSA recalculates your benefit upward once you reach full retirement age to credit you for months when payments were reduced.
 3. The maximum benefit for workers retiring at full retirement age increases
The SSA also adjusts the maximum possible benefit figures each year to reflect wage growth and the COLA. For a worker retiring at FRA in 2027, the maximum monthly benefit rises to $4,188, up from $4,152 in 2026, according to the SSA's 2027 fact sheet.
It's important to understand what this number does and doesn't represent. This is the ceiling for someone claiming at FRA specifically, not the largest benefit available overall. Workers who delay claiming until age 70 can receive meaningfully more, since delayed retirement credits add roughly 8% per year to your benefit for each year you wait past FRA, up to age 70. 
 The SSA's figures show a worker retiring at age 70 in 2026 could receive up to $5,181 per month, compared with $4,152 for someone claiming at FRA that same year, illustrating just how much claiming age affects the math. Either way, hitting the maximum at any claiming age requires earning at or above the taxable maximum in each of roughly 35 working years, not simply working for 35 years.

 4. Social Security's taxable maximum rises to $192,300 in 2027
Social Security taxes only apply to wages up to a certain cap, known as the taxable maximum or contribution and benefit base. For 2027, that cap rises to $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026, the SSA confirms.
This change affects a relatively narrow slice of workers: those earning more than $184,500 in 2027. If you're one of them, more of your income becomes subject to the 6.2% Social Security payroll tax (the employer pays a matching 6.2%). Someone earning at or above the new cap would pay $11,922.60 into OASDI (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance) in 2027, matched by an equal employer contribution, according to the SSA. Self-employed workers face the combined 12.4% rate on earnings up to the cap.
For most workers, who earn well under $184,500, this change has no effect on their paychecks at all. It's a cost increase targeted at higher earners, not a broad-based tax hike.
 5. Earning a Social Security credit requires more income in 2027
To qualify for Social Security benefits down the road, you need to accumulate 40 work credits over your lifetime, with a maximum of four credits available per year. The amount of earnings required for one credit, known as a quarter of coverage, rises to $1,970 in 2027, up from $1,890 in 2026, per the SSA.
This mostly matters for younger workers, part-time workers, or people with gaps in their earnings history who are still building toward the 40-credit threshold needed for retirement eligibility. For most people already fully insured, this change is mostly academic. But it's a reminder that the bar for qualifying for benefits in the first place also moves with wage growth, not just the dollar amounts attached to benefits themselves.
 6. Disability thresholds rise too, affecting SSDI and SSI applicants
A few disability-related thresholds are climbing in 2027 as well. The substantial gainful activity (SGA) limit, the earnings level the SSA uses to determine whether someone is engaging in meaningful work activity despite a disability, rises to $1,770 per month for non-blind individuals, up from $1,690 in 2026, and $2,950 per month for blind individuals, up from $2,830 in 2026, according to the SSA.
The trial work period threshold, which lets Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) beneficiaries test their ability to work without immediately losing benefits, increases to $1,270 per month in 2027, up from $1,210 in 2026. These adjustments give disabled workers and SSDI beneficiaries a bit more room to earn before it affects their benefit status.

 7. SSI payment standards and resource rules get modest increases
For SSI recipients, the federal payment standard, the maximum monthly SSI benefit for someone with no other countable income, rises to $1,029 for an individual and $1,544 for a couple in 2027, up from $994 and $1,491, respectively, in 2026, the SSA reports.
One thing that isn't changing: the SSI resource limits remain frozen at $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple, unchanged for years. These limits determine how many assets someone can hold and still qualify for SSI, and they're not indexed to inflation the way other figures are. That means the real-world value of what counts as "too many assets" to qualify keeps eroding over time, a detail that's easy to overlook amid the other increases.
 Bottom line
The 2027 COLA headline number, 3.6%, is only part of what's changing for Social Security next year. Earnings-test limits are rising, which is good news for working beneficiaries under FRA. The maximum benefit for workers retiring at FRA is increasing too. But the taxable maximum is also climbing, which means higher earners will pay Social Security tax on a larger share of their income.
The SSA's online benefit calculators and a my Social Security account can show estimates based on an individual's actual earnings record. Reviewing a benefit statement periodically, especially as thresholds shift each year, can help you  maximize your senior benefits and clarify where things stand before making any claiming decisions.
